You sure it isn't just buffering from loading the area? Consider this, whenever you teleport or spawn, the game needs to create visuals up all of the chunks in your render distance at once, rather than just a handful of new ones as you travel on foot. What I mean by this distinction is simple: suppose that you have a render distance of 2 chunks, which means that in order to accompany you, the game loads two chunks in each direction, giving the total number of chunks to be 25. Now, keeping this in mind, assume that you walk straight north. Whenever the game sees that your short on render distance, it will load the visuals for chunks inside of your new render distance, and unload the chunks outside of it, meaning that as you transition chunks, you will be loading the visuals for (or "rendering") 5 chunks and unloading that same amount. Because this is relatively a smaller amount of change, it makes the game appear to let the player walk around the world more smoothly and without any seeming "lag." When you teleport or spawn, it would need to unload any renders that it had previously had loaded, and fill in the missing space. While 25 doesn't seem like a lot for modern computing, go do the math with some higher numbers like a distance of 7 ((7*2+1)^2 = 225!) and you can see that it works quite a bit. So, in addition to transitioning the player's location on the server and communicating it to the client, the client must also also render all of the visuals at the same time.

Knowing this (if I had to take a rough guess), I'd say that the game's "loading" is the communication taking place that takes place between the client and server to "register" the transition in coordinates and/or plane (since all modern maps have at least three realms). Meanwhile, the game attempts to render the area while allowing the player to move around (which wouldn't be unbelievable if it uses the same methods of chunk rendering as normal traveling to allow the player to navigate without "lag"). As the renders are finished, the game corrects the player and any mobs' positions to prevent this from being exploited or kill the player by letting them fall into the void. Again, this is a guess, so if anyone sees anything that I got wrong with it, please feel free to correct me.

There really isn't a solid way to fix this that I know of, but helping reduce the amount of content that needs to be rendered may help, including distance and mobs, but this means that you really need to know the area that you're spawning in. Otherwise, the only real harm that this would usually do is inconvenience you while you wait (assuming that you have your teleport locations in a secure and safe place, right?).
